messages.body_plain:
I had a similar situation: my solution may not be the prettiest, but it works.

My data was already read into R as a data frame, with a separate column for each taxonomic level. I created a column with the merged taxonomy, like this:
> taxbactprop$mergetax<-paste(taxbact$Kingdom,"|",taxbact$Phylum,"|",taxbact$Class,"|",taxbact$Order,"|",taxbact$Family,"|",taxbact$Genus,"|",taxbact$Species)

I then exported this dataframe as a .csv and read it back in:
> write.csv(taxbactprop,"taxbactprop.csv",quote = FALSE)
> bacttaxmap<-parse_taxonomy_table("taxbactprop.csv", taxon_col = c("class" = -1),
                                 other_col_type="obs_info", sep=",",
                                 class_sep = "\\|")

This creates a taxmap object ready for subsequent use in metacoder!

messages.subject: Re: Taxonomic information already extracted
messages.body_plain:
No problem! So I can see two ways to do this:

1) You have a few ranks of the taxonomy distributed over a few columns. I see most rows have family, genus, and species. This is enough information to make a heat tree, but it will only have 4 levels (if you add a universal "root" taxon). It looks like these are all mammals? If so you can provide a better name than "root", such as "Mammalia", or whatever is the least coarse rank that applies to all of you data. The functions in metacoder for parsing data assume that all taxonomic information is together (e.g. Mammalia;Felidae;Felis;catus), so you would have to make a new column that is a combination of the `family_name`, `genus_name`, and `species_name` columns and feed that into `parse_taxonomy_table`.

2) The first table you sent me had a taxon id, which I assume is an NCBI taxonomy database ID? If that is the case, the parsing functions can look up the taxonomy by querying NCBI online. However, NCBI's databases are seriously slow sometimes, so this is not always practical. However, this requires much less code and no reformatting of the data. How many rows are there? Or more importantly, how many unique taxon IDs are there? This would give you all levels of the taxonomy, but you might only need the ones you already have if they are all mammals.

Anyway, I am going to assume that option 1 will work better, so I made sure that it would work by doing it. Attached is an compressed R project with an analysis in an Rmd file. I also attached the resultant PDF separately. Let me know if you have more questions or comments.

messages.subject: Re: Overlapping node labels
messages.body_plain:
Hi Sarah,

Overlapping node labels have been a constant annoyance for me as well. I would like to add a `jitter` option, but I have been putting it off since doing it well could be tricky. A simple random jitter would be easy and perhaps a little useful, but trying to actually avoid overlaps would be harder. I have made an issue on the GitHub site in regards to this:

https://github.com/grunwaldlab/metacoder/issues/136

If you follow the issue, you will get updates when it is done.
In the mean time, here are a couple strategies I use to avoid label overlaps.

* Depending on the graph and how long labels are, you can use edge labels with the `edge_label` option. These are less likely to overlap, but are usually smaller. You can also do a combination of the two like i did in the HMP analysis <https://grunwaldlab.github.io/metacoder_documentation/publication--05--16s_human_microbiome.html>.
* Use fewer labels. Not ideal, but probably the easiest solution.
* Use smaller labels. Also not ideal, but easy.
* If it is an important figure that is worth some customization, you can selectively rename or omit node labels with something like `node_label = ifelse(name %in% labels_to_omit, "", name)` where `labels_to_omit = c("A label that is just really too long", "another label to omit")`
* Try a different layout. I find that using `layout = "da", initial_layout = "re"` can spread things out nicely and since this has a random component, every time the graph is made it will look different unless you set a seed before running the graph each time with `
set.seed(7)`. If its worth the effort, you can try different seeds until you find one that spreads out the nodes well. You can fiddle with the options for `?igraph::layout.davidson.harel` if its close but not quite right.

Hope that helps a bit. I will update this when/if I add a `jitter` option.

messages.subject: Re: Including statistics calculated previously
messages.body_plain:
Hi Andre,

Im glad you like the package! Thanks!

I have attached an example analysis as a PDF and the compressed R project containing the Rmd that produced it.
All the info is in there, but the summary is:

Any column in `data$taxon_data` or function in `data$taxon_funcs` can be used for filtering/plotting taxa, so you can use already calcuolated info by adding it as a column to `data$taxon_data`. However, the `Percentage`  column is in `data$obs_data`, so you need to use `obs` to assign a "percentage" to each taxon. I did this by averaging all the percentages for each taxon. Once the data is in `data$taxon_data`, it can be used for filtering.

Let me know if you have more questions or have any issues with the attached files,

-Zach

## Parse data
library(metacoder)
raw_data <- read.csv("FunctionsTest.csv", header = TRUE)
data <- parse_taxonomy_table(raw_data, taxon_col = c("class" = -1), class_sep = "\\|")

## Calculate average percentage
data <- mutate_taxa(data,
                    mean_percentage = sapply(obs(data), function(i) mean(data$obs_data$Percentage[i])))

## Filtering taxa and labels
data %>%
  filter_taxa(mean_percentage > 0.1, supertaxa = TRUE) %>% # Remove taxa
  heat_tree(node_size = n_obs,
            edge_color = mean_percentage,
            node_color = mean_percentage,
            node_label = ifelse(mean_percentage > 0.3, name, NA), # Selectivly display labels

            overlap_avoidance = 0.5,
            node_color_range = c("cyan", "magenta", "green"),
            edge_color_range   = c("#555555", "#EEEEEE"),
            node_label_max = 500,
            initial_layout = "reingold-tilford", layout = "davidson-harel")

messages.subject: Re: Output of selected taxonomic ranks for sequences in taxmap object
messages.subject_clean: Output of selected taxonomic ranks for sequences in taxmap object
messages.body_plain:
Hi Royce,

Without seeing your data I cant say for sure, but I can imagine a few strategies, depend on whether you want to filter the object, or just add a column  in the obs_data table without filtering. There is no dedicated function to do this kind of thing yet, but I have some in mind that probably will be added in the next big update.

Both strategies use the `supertaxa` function, which returns the supertaxa for each taxon. You can make the function return taxon indexes (for `taxon_data`) using `index = TRUE` and include the target taxon in the list by `include_input = TRUE`. This is what we will be looping over:

library(metacoder)
supertaxa(unite_ex_data_1, index = TRUE, include_input = TRUE)

note that `unite_ex_data_1` is an included data set, so you can try this code.

Filtering taxa by rank:

data <- unite_ex_data_1
allowed_ranks <- c("kingdom", "phylum", "class",  "order", "family", "genus", "species")
data <- filter_taxa(data, rank %in% allowed_ranks)
data <- mutate_taxa(data, all_ranks = sapply(supertaxa(data, index = TRUE, include_input = TRUE),
                                             function(i) paste0(data$taxon_data$rank[rev(i)], collapse = ";")))

Only use some ranks, but dont filter:

data <- unite_ex_data_1
allowed_ranks <- c("kingdom", "phylum", "class",  "order", "family", "genus", "species")
data <- mutate_taxa(data, all_ranks = sapply(supertaxa(data, index = TRUE, include_input = TRUE),
                                             function(i) {
                                                 valid_ranks <- data$taxon_data$rank[rev(i)]
                                                 valid_ranks <- valid_ranks[valid_ranks %in% allowed_ranks]
                                                 paste0(valid_ranks, collapse = ";")
                                             }))

Mapping back to observations:

After either method, you can map the taxon data to the observations like so:

data$obs_data$all_ranks <- data$taxon_data$all_ranks[match(data$obs_data$obs_taxon_ids, data$taxon_data$taxon_ids)]

Hope this helps. Let me know if you have more questions or ideas for functions you would like to be added.

messages.body_plain:
Thank you so much Zachary, that helped a lot. I was not clear that I wanted the actual taxonomic rank names ('Metazoa' rather than  'Kingdom' for example) so I just changed 'rank' to 'name' (see highlight below) which ultimately enabled me to accomplish what I wanted, which was to write a fasta file with the seqinr package containing the taxonomic lineage in the fasta headers.

cheers,
Royce

##################################################################
data <- genbank_ex_data

allowed_ranks <- c("kingdom", "phylum", "class",
                   "order", "family", "genus", "species")

data <- filter_taxa(data, rank %in% allowed_ranks)

data <- mutate_taxa(data, all_ranks = sapply(supertaxa(data,
              index = TRUE, include_input = TRUE),

              function(i) paste0(data$taxon_data$name[rev(i)],
              collapse = ";")))

### Mapping back to observations############

data$obs_data$all_ranks <- data$taxon_data$all_ranks[match(data$obs_data$obs_taxon_ids,
                        data$taxon_data$taxon_ids)]
